entries.title: What is a nostro overdraft?
entries.text: A nostro overdraft happens when a bank instructs its correspondent to pay out more money from a nostro account than the account actually holds, so the balance goes negative. Because the correspondent has already paid the beneficiary, it has effectively lent the bank money for a short period, usually until the bank sends funds to cover the shortfall. entries.title: What does a treasury team do with payment flows during the day?
entries.text: Treasury manages the bank's money so that payments can settle on time. Every morning treasury looks at the nostro balances, the expected payment volumes for the day and the funding available. They decide how much liquidity to hold in each currency and each account. During the day, treasury watches the balances in real time. If a large payment is about to go out and the nostro balance is low,

entries.title: How does a bank manage liquidity for payments across time zones?
entries.text: A global bank operates in many time zones, and money is needed in different places at different times. Treasury manages this by planning the day in sequence. The day starts in Asia, where payments go out in the morning. Treasury makes sure the Asian nostro accounts are funded before the Asian business day starts. entries.title: The treasury team needs to fund the bank's central bank settlement account before the morning clearing window. How does that funding happen, and what if the balance is short?
entries.text: The bank holds a **settlement account** at the central bank, and every **RTGS** payment settles across it in real time. Treasury forecasts the day's outflows the evening before, using the payment queue, standing instructions, and expected client payments. entries.title: Explain intraday liquidity. How does a bank make sure it has enough funds in its central bank account to settle payments through the day?
entries.text: **Intraday liquidity** is the cash the bank needs in its **central bank settlement account** during the day to settle **RTGS** payments as they arrive. Because RTGS settles each payment gross in real time, the bank cannot wait until the end of the day to fund. It needs the money available when each payment is released. entries.title: How does a bank fund its nostro accounts, and how does treasury decide how much to hold in each currency?
entries.text: A **nostro account** is an account the bank holds with a correspondent bank in a foreign currency, and it is how the bank pays in currencies where it has no central bank account. Treasury funds each nostro by forecasting the day's outflows in that currency, looking at the payment queue, expected client payments, and known large transactions. entries.title: A high-value payment needs to go out but the bank's intraday liquidity is tight. What options does the bank have?
entries.text: When intraday liquidity is tight, the bank has four levers. First, it can borrow from the central bank's **intraday liquidity facility** against eligible collateral, usually government bonds. This is the normal first step and it is designed for exactly this situation. The bank pledges collateral, receives funds in its **settlement account**, and repays before the end of the day. entries.title: How does the bank prioritise payments in a queue when liquidity is limited? Which payments go first and why?
entries.text: When liquidity is limited, the bank does not release payments in the order they arrived. It prioritises. The first priority is payments to a clearing house or a central bank, because failing to settle those can suspend the bank from the clearing system. The second priority is time-critical client payments, such as **CHAPS** payments near cut-off, property completions, and payroll. The third

entries.text: The payment settled, but the bank is flying blind. The **Nostro ledger** is the bank's own eyes on its foreign currency positions, and Treasury is now making funding decisions from stale data. This is critical. entries.text: Intraday liquidity is the money the bank needs available during the day to settle payments as they arrive. The design has two parts: **monitoring** and **management**. For monitoring, the hub reports every payment it is about to send to the **liquidity management system**, which tracks the expected outflow against the balance in the settlement account. entries.title: How does a bank manage liquidity and Nostro funding so that every payment settles on time? Walk through a day in the Treasury function.
entries.text: Liquidity management works when Treasury can see the position in real time and fund it before the cut-off. The bank holds **Nostro accounts** with correspondent banks in every currency it settles in. As payments flow out during the day, the Nostro balance falls. As payments flow in, it rises. entries.title: It is 2 PM and the nostro balance in US dollars is running low. Payments are queuing in the hub and the next funding will not arrive until tomorrow. What does the treasury team do right now?
entries.text: The treasury team acts immediately, because a nostro account with no balance means payments **stop**. First, they check the exact balance and the **queue**: how many payments are waiting, what their total value is, and which ones are urgent. Second, they look for **funds elsewhere**: another nostro account in the same currency, a balance that can be moved, or a **FX swap** that converts another

entries.title: Your bank has a large FX payment settling through CLS. The pay-in deadline is in 30 minutes and the bank is short of the required currency. Explain what CLS is, why the deadline matters, and what happens if the bank misses it.
entries.text: **CLS**, Continuous Linked Settlement, is the system that settles **FX trades** between banks. It removes **settlement risk**, the risk that one side pays and the other side does not, by settling both sides of the trade at the same time, on a payment versus payment basis. Each bank must **pay in** the currency it sold by a strict deadline, and CLS then pays out the currency it bought. The

entries.title: A bank needs to settle a large CHAPS payment but does not have enough balance in its Bank of England settlement account. Explain intraday liquidity, how the bank gets it, and what collateral is involved.
entries.text: **Intraday liquidity** is the money a bank needs during the day to settle payments before its own receipts arrive. A bank may be perfectly solvent but still short of cash at 10 AM, because its incoming payments arrive later than its outgoing payments. entries.title: Your bank holds liquidity in five currencies, but most of it is trapped in Japanese yen while the urgent payments are in US dollars. Explain trapped liquidity, why it happens, and how the treasury team frees it up.
entries.text: **Trapped liquidity** is money that exists but cannot be used where it is needed. The bank holds a large balance in **Japanese yen**, but the urgent payments are in **US dollars**, and the yen cannot be spent on a dollar payment. It happens because liquidity is held in separate **nostro accounts** in different countries and different currencies, and moving it takes time, costs money, and depends

entries.title: It is month end and payment volumes are 40 percent higher than normal. The treasury team needs to fund the settlement account for the morning clearing window. Walk through how they prepare.
entries.text: Month end is the busiest day in payments, because **salaries**, **supplier payments**, and **tax payments** all fall on the same day. The treasury team prepares the day before. First, they take the **forecast**: the expected volume and value of outgoing payments, based on previous month ends and on the payment files already received from corporate customers. entries.title: A corporate customer notices that small charges are being deducted from their nostro account every month, and the balance is slowly falling. Explain what nostro charges are, why they appear, and how the customer forecasts them.
entries.text: **Nostro charges** are the fees the correspondent bank deducts for holding and operating the **nostro account**. They include **account maintenance** fees, charges for each payment processed, fees for statements and reporting, and charges for investigations or repairs. The correspondent bank deducts them directly from the nostro balance, usually monthly, which is why the balance falls slowly even

entries.title: Several large payments are stuck in the RTGS queue because no bank has enough balance to settle. The queue is not clearing and the central bank intervenes. Explain RTGS gridlock and how queue resolution works.
entries.text: **Gridlock** happens in a **real time gross settlement** system when several banks are each waiting for an incoming payment before they can send their own outgoing payment, and nobody can move first. Bank A is waiting for money from Bank B, Bank B is waiting for money from Bank C, and Bank C is waiting for money from Bank A. No single bank is short of money overall, but each one is short right

entries.title: The treasury forecasting model predicted 500 million in outgoing payments today, but the actual volume is 700 million. The settlement account is underfunded. Explain what went wrong and how the team recovers and fixes the model.
entries.text: A forecast that is wrong by **40 percent** usually has a specific cause, not a random error. The first step is to find it: did a large corporate customer send a payment file that was not in the forecast, did a **value date** change move payments from tomorrow to today, or did the model use the wrong day, such as treating a month end Monday as a normal Monday. entries.title: What is a payment recall?
entries.text: A payment recall is a request by the sending bank to cancel a payment that has already been sent and to return the funds. It is used when the payment was sent by mistake, for example to the wrong beneficiary, for the wrong amount, or in duplicate, or when the underlying transaction has been cancelled. The recall is sent as a message through the same network that carried the original payment,

entries.title: What is a payment return?
entries.text: A payment return is when a payment that was sent to a beneficiary bank is sent back to the sender because it cannot be applied. Unlike a recall, which is initiated by the sender, a return is usually initiated by the beneficiary bank or an intermediary bank that cannot complete the payment. The most common reasons for a return are incorrect beneficiary details, such as a wrong account number or a

entries.title: What is a nostro account reconciliation?
entries.text: Nostro account reconciliation is the daily process of matching every entry on a nostro account statement from the correspondent bank against the bank own internal records, to prove that the two agree. The bank downloads the statement from, say, Wells Fargo for its US dollar nostro account, and compares each debit and credit with its own ledger. Items that match are cleared. Items that do not

entries.title: What is a recall (camt.056) and when is it used?
entries.text: A recall is a request by the sender bank to the beneficiary bank to return a payment that has already been sent, and in ISO 20022 it is carried by the camt.056 message, the FI to FI Payment Cancellation Request. A recall is used when the sender has made a mistake, for example sending a duplicate payment, sending the wrong amount, sending to the wrong beneficiary, or sending a payment that was

entries.title: What is a payment repair?
entries.text: A payment repair is the manual work done to fix a payment that cannot be processed automatically because it has an error, missing data, or an unclear instruction. When a payment arrives at a bank and fails straight through processing, it is moved to a repair queue, where an operations analyst reviews it and decides what to do. entries.title: What is a payment amendment and how is it processed?
entries.text: A payment amendment is a change to a payment instruction after it has been sent but before it has been finally settled, for example correcting a beneficiary name, changing an account number, updating a remittance reference, or changing the value date. Amendments are needed when the sender spots an error, or when the beneficiary asks for a correction, and they are processed through a formal

entries.title: How does a reconciliation API work? How do a bank and its corporate partner compare their payment records at end of day?
entries.text: A **reconciliation API** lets the bank and its partners compare their records automatically. The flow is: at end of day, the hub generates a **reconciliation file** listing every payment it processed, with the payment ID, the amount, the currency, the status, and the settlement reference. The partner downloads the file through an API endpoint and compares it against their own records. Any payment

entries.title: How does a bank reconcile payments at end of day?
entries.text: Reconciliation is the daily check that every payment the bank sent actually settled, and every payment it received actually arrived. The reconciliation team starts with three lists: what the payment hub sent, what the clearing system confirmed and what the core banking system posted to customer accounts. They match these three lists against each other. A payment that appears on all three lists is

entries.title: What happens when a payment is sent to the wrong account at a large bank?
entries.text: A payment sent to the wrong account is one of the hardest problems in payments because the money has already moved. First, the bank checks what happened: was the account number wrong, did the customer type it incorrectly, or did the bank map it wrong. entries.text: At the end of the day, the bank must prove its **central bank settlement account** balance matches what the central bank says it is. The operations team pulls the central bank statement, usually a **camt.053** or the central bank's own statement, and compares it line by line against the bank's own ledger. entries.title: A cross-border payment is rejected before settlement and the receiving bank sends back a pacs.002 with RJCT status and a reason code. No funds have moved. What do you do?
entries.text: A **pacs.002** with RJCT status is a pre-settlement rejection, so the first fact I establish is that no money has moved. That single fact decides the whole path, because this is repair and resubmit, not a return. I read the **reason code** carefully, because it tells me exactly what failed. entries.text: The engine and the clearing layer apply different rules, so the instructed amount and the settled amount can legitimately differ. My job is to find exactly which rule changed it, and whether that rule was supposed to apply. entries.title: A customer is waiting for a 125,000 pound international payment. The sender confirms it left, the beneficiary bank says it never arrived. There is no rejection, no return, no confirmation. How do you investigate?
entries.text: When nobody can say where the money is, I prove what happened before I act. A blind re-send would risk a duplicate, which is worse than a delay. I first classify the investigation, because a payment that clearly failed needs a different approach from one where nobody can yet prove what happened. entries.title: A duplicate payment has gone out. The retry fired after a timeout and the system sent the same payment twice. The customer has been paid twice. What is your response?
entries.text: The first move is to **stop the bleed**. I freeze the retry and payout batch immediately so no more duplicates go out while I investigate. Then I identify the full population, every payout that went twice, matched by reference or **idempotency key**. entries.text: A payment sent to the wrong IBAN is not a failed payment, it is a successful payment to the wrong person. That distinction matters, because the recovery is a recall, not a retry. I start by confirming settlement, an **ACSC** status on the pacs.002 chain, which tells me the funds have actually moved. entries.text: A recall after credit is a request, not a command. The beneficiary bank decides, and the money only moves if it accepts. The sender bank sends a **camt.056 cancellation request** down the chain to the beneficiary bank. The beneficiary bank checks two things. Are the funds still available in the account, and is there any fraud concern. The decision comes back in a **camt.029**, accept or reject,

entries.text: No. A timeout means I do not know the outcome, and a blind retry can double-pay. I **freeze the payment** and block any automatic retry until the true state is established. Then I investigate with the **UETR, EndToEndId, and TxId** across the gpi Tracker and the internal hop logs. entries.title: A pacs.004 return was expected three days ago but it never arrived. The original payment settled, the beneficiary bank said it would return the funds, and now there is silence. What do you do?
entries.text: A return that never arrives is an open item, and open items age badly. I start by confirming the original payment settled, using the **ACSC** status on the pacs.002 chain. Then I check whether the return was actually initiated. I look for the **pacs.004** in the message logs, and I check the gpi Tracker with the original UETR to see if a return leg exists. entries.title: A corporate customer calls, angry, because a 500,000 euro payment to a supplier has not arrived after two days. The supplier is threatening to stop deliveries. How do you handle this complaint?
entries.text: The customer is angry because they have no information, not just because the money is late. So the first job is to get facts fast and communicate them. I take the payment reference and the **UETR** and check the **gpi Tracker** immediately, because the last confirmed hop tells me where the payment is. entries.text: The beneficiary bank discovered the problem, so it becomes the return originator and sends the **pacs.004** itself. It does not wait for the sender to ask. The trigger is found post-credit, a closed account, a frozen account, or a similar problem discovered after the funds landed. entries.text: The payment was debited but the credit never arrived, so first confirm the debit actually happened by checking the **core banking posting**. Then check the **pacs.002** chain. entries.title: How do you reconcile payments between the payment hub, the core banking system and the clearing house? What are the common breaks?
entries.text: Reconciliation between the hub and the core is a **three way match**. At end of day, you compare three sources: the **payment hub ledger** (every instruction the hub accepted), the **core banking postings** (every debit and credit the core recorded), and the **clearing house confirmations** (every payment the clearing house settled). entries.text: Clean reconciliation means the books agree, and it works because the comparison happens continuously, not once a month. The payment hub records every payment it sends, with the amount, the value date, and the status. entries.text: A clean end-of-day works because the statement and the books are compared the same day, not the next morning. The correspondent bank sends a **camt.053** statement at the end of the business day, listing every debit and credit on the Nostro account. entries.text: A clean cross-border payment with full remittance data works because the beneficiary can reconcile it without a phone call. The customer sends a **pain.001** with the full remittance information, the invoice number, the purchase order, and the payment reference, all in the structured fields. entries.text: **ACCP** means the payment has been accepted by the clearing system or the next bank in the chain, and it is being processed. It does not mean the money has settled yet. It means the payment passed validation, the account exists, and the payment is on its way. entries.title: A pacs.002 comes back with RJCT. Walk me through the handling step by step.
entries.text: **RJCT** means the payment has been rejected before settlement, and no money has moved. That is the most important fact, because it means the fix is repair and resubmit, not a return. The first step is to read the **pacs.002** carefully. It carries a reason code that tells the bank exactly what failed, for example an invalid account number, a sanctions flag, or a formatting error. entries.text: The first step is to trust the **ACSC** status but verify it. ACSC means the clearing system confirmed settlement, so the funds left the bank. The operations team pulls the settlement confirmation and checks the amount, currency, value date, and beneficiary account against the original instruction. entries.title: How does the bank reconcile its payment ledger against the camt.053 statement from its account servicer?
entries.text: The **camt.053** is the account statement the bank receives from its account servicer, usually a correspondent bank or the central bank. It lists every debit and credit on the account for the period, with references. entries.title: A camt.054 debit notification arrives but there is no matching payment in the hub. What do you do?
entries.text: A **camt.054** is a debit or credit notification. It tells the bank that money has moved on its account, and it arrives separately from the statement. When a camt.054 debit arrives with no matching payment in the hub, the first step is to check whether it is a charge, a fee, or a settlement adjustment, rather than a customer payment. entries.title: The bank sent 1,000 payments today but only received 995 pacs.002 responses. How do you chase the missing five?
entries.text: The **payment hub** tracks every payment it sends and expects a **pacs.002** response for each one. At the end of the settlement window, the hub runs a check that lists every payment still waiting for a response. The operations team works through the list. For each missing response, the team checks whether the payment actually settled by looking at the clearing confirmation and the **camt.053**

entries.title: A duplicate pacs.002 arrives for a payment that is already ACSC. How does the bank handle it without double-posting?
entries.text: A duplicate **pacs.002** is not unusual. The clearing system or an intermediary may send the same status twice, especially after a retry or a system recovery. The **payment hub** must handle it without double-posting. entries.text: This is a status synchronisation problem between the **payment hub** and the **channel**. The hub is the system of record, so the ACSC status in the hub is correct. The channel, which is what the customer sees, has not received the update. The first step is to confirm the hub status is genuinely ACSC by checking the settlement confirmation. entries.text: The first step is to confirm the break is real and not a timing difference. The team checks the value date and the settlement time. If the debit is in the ledger but the clearing confirmation has not arrived yet, it may simply be that the confirmation is still in transit, and the break will clear itself. entries.text: **AC01** means the account number is incorrect. The **pacs.002** carries this reason code, and it tells the bank the beneficiary account number in the instruction does not match any account at the beneficiary bank. entries.text: An unexpected credit on the **camt.053** means money arrived in the bank's account that the bank was not expecting. The reconciliation team must identify it before it can be posted correctly. The first step is to read the statement line carefully. entries.title: How does the bank reconcile nostro accounts using MT950 or camt.053, and what are the common breaks?
entries.text: **Nostro reconciliation** is the daily check that the bank's own record of its **nostro account**, the account it holds with a correspondent bank in a foreign currency, matches the correspondent bank's record. The bank receives a statement, usually an **MT950** or a **camt.053**, from the correspondent and compares each line against its own nostro ledger. A match needs the same amount, currency,

entries.title: A value date mismatch appears between the pacs.008 the bank sent and the settlement confirmation. How do you resolve it?
entries.text: A **value date** mismatch means the bank expected the payment to settle on one date but the settlement confirmation shows a different date. The first step is to check the original instruction. The **pacs.008** carries the requested execution date, and the hub should have applied the correct value date based on the clearing calendar and the cut-off. If the hub applied the wrong value date, for

entries.title: The bank receives a pacs.002 with a status it does not recognise. What is the handling?
entries.text: When a **pacs.002** arrives with a status the hub does not recognise, the hub should not crash and it should not ignore the message. It should park the message in an exception queue and alert the operations team. The team reads the raw pacs.002 and identifies the status code. It may be a new status introduced by the clearing system, a proprietary status from an intermediary, or a code the hub's

entries.title: An investigation is opened with a camt.056 for a payment the beneficiary says never arrived. Walk through the investigation.
entries.text: When a beneficiary says a payment never arrived, the bank opens a formal investigation. The first step is to check the bank's own records. The **payment hub** shows the status, and the settlement confirmation shows whether the funds left the bank. entries.title: A reconciliation item sits in the suspense account for three days. What is the process to clear it, and who owns it?
entries.text: A **suspense account** is where the bank parks money it cannot yet explain. When a reconciliation item sits in suspense for three days, it is already overdue. The reconciliation team owns the item and must clear it. The first step is to re-investigate. entries.title: The bank's auto-reconciliation matches 98 percent of items. What happens to the other 2 percent, and how are they worked?
entries.text: **Auto-reconciliation** matches most items automatically, usually 95 to 99 percent, because most payments match on amount, currency, value date, and reference. The remaining 2 percent do not match, and they are the ones that need human attention. The reconciliation system puts the unmatched items in an exceptions queue, and the reconciliation team works through them. Each exception is one of a

entries.title: A customer is charged a fee that does not match the charge option on the pacs.008. How do you investigate and correct it?
entries.text: The charge option on the **pacs.008** tells the banks in the chain who pays the fees. **OUR** means the sender pays all charges, **SHA** means the sender and the beneficiary share them, and **BEN** means the beneficiary pays them all. When the customer is charged a fee that does not match the charge option, the first step is to check the pacs.008 and confirm what was instructed. Then the team

entries.title: How does end-of-day reconciliation sign-off work, and what happens if the team cannot sign off?
entries.text: **End-of-day reconciliation sign-off** is the formal confirmation that the bank's books balance for the day. The reconciliation team checks that every payment sent and received is accounted for, that the **nostro** accounts reconcile to the correspondent statements, that the **central bank settlement account** matches the central bank's record, and that the **suspense account** contains no

entries.title: A pacs.002 arrives after the bank has already sent a pacs.004 return for the same payment. How do you resolve the conflict?
entries.text: This is a conflict that should not happen, but it does. A **pacs.004** return means the bank already sent the money back, but a **pacs.002** arriving afterwards says something about the original payment's status. The **payment hub** must handle this carefully. The hub checks the sequence. If the pacs.004 was already sent and the return is in progress, the pacs.002 is usually a late status update

entries.title: A duplicate payment is sent because the channel submitted it twice. How does the bank detect it, stop the second one, and recover the funds if it settled?
entries.text: A duplicate payment usually happens when the **channel** submits the same instruction twice, for example because the customer clicked submit twice, or because the channel retried a submission after a timeout without checking whether the first one went through. The **payment hub** should catch it. The hub checks each incoming instruction against recent payments using the customer, the amount, the

entries.title: How does the bank reconcile charges and fees deducted by correspondent banks against what was instructed in the pacs.008?
entries.text: When a payment travels through correspondent banks, each bank in the chain can deduct a fee. The **pacs.008** carries the charge option, **OUR**, **SHA**, or **BEN**, and the instructed amount. The bank reconciles the charges by comparing three things. First, what was instructed in the pacs.008. Second, what the correspondent deducted, as shown on the **camt.053** statement and the **camt.054**

entries.title: A payment is sent twice by mistake. How do you handle it?
entries.text: A duplicate payment is serious because the beneficiary has been paid twice and the bank may not get the second payment back easily. First, I confirm it is a real duplicate: same amount, same beneficiary, same reference, sent twice. I check whether both payments settled or only one did. Second, I stop any further duplicates: I check if the source system is sending the payment twice, if a retry

entries.title: What is sanctions screening?
entries.text: Sanctions screening is the process of checking every party and detail in a payment against lists of people, companies, countries, and vessels that governments have sanctioned. If a payment involves a sanctioned person or country, the bank must not process it, or must process it only under a specific licence. Screening happens before the payment is released, and it is one of the most important

entries.title: How does a bank handle a sanctions hit on a payment?
entries.text: When a payment hits a sanctions list, the system stops it automatically before it leaves the bank. No one can override this by hand. The payment goes to a sanctions queue where a compliance analyst reviews it. The analyst checks the name, the address and the details of the payment against the sanctions list to decide if it is a true match or a false positive. A false positive is common: a

entries.title: A payment is sent to a bank in a country under sanctions screening. It is held at the clearing stage. Walk through what happens next.
entries.text: When a payment is held at the clearing stage for **sanctions screening**, it means a name, a country, or a word in the payment matched a sanctions list or a screening rule. The payment does not fail, it is held for review. The bank's compliance team receives the alert and investigates. They check the names against the sanctions lists, look at the full payment details, and decide whether the match

entries.title: A payment is held mid-flight because the beneficiary name fuzzy-matches a sanctions list. It could be a real hit or a false positive. What happens next?
entries.text: The payment is held immediately and no funds move while the review is open. That is the first rule, because a held payment can be released but a released payment cannot be un-sent. The analyst escalates to the **compliance officer** with the match evidence attached, including which list matched, the match score, and the payment details. Then comes **true-match verification**. The compliance team

entries.title: Screening flags the ultimate beneficiary details as doubtful, but not definitively wrong. Do you reject the payment immediately or investigate first?
entries.text: When the data is doubtful but not definitively wrong, I ask before I kill the payment. I park it, request the information, and decide on facts. An instant reject could kill a legitimate payment, and a wrongly rejected payment damages the customer relationship. I send a **request for additional information** back up the chain to the sender bank, asking for the specific detail that is unclear. I

entries.title: A letter of credit worth 28 million dirhams is delayed eight working days because sanctions screening fuzzy-matched a common surname. There is no fraud and no real risk, just bad screening logic. How do you fix false positives without missing real hits?
entries.text: About 95 percent of sanctions alerts are false positives, but every one still delays real business. The client in this case faced **cash-flow strain** because a legitimate letter of credit sat parked for eight working days on a common surname match. I fix it by **triaging by risk**. Exact matches and high-risk corridors get senior review first. Common-name matches go through a fast lane with a

entries.title: A 500,000 dollar wire is blocked when the beneficiary name fuzzy-matches the OFAC SDN list. The analyst escalates to compliance, the payment is held, and a SAR is filed. Walk through what happens.
entries.text: The payment is held immediately when **screening flags** the beneficiary name as a fuzzy match against the SDN list. No funds move while the review is open. The analyst **escalates to the compliance officer** with the match evidence attached, including the list entry, the match score, and the full payment details. Then comes **true-match verification**. The compliance team compares the

entries.title: Transaction monitoring flags multiple accounts. The pattern is small inward transfers from unrelated sources, funds moved out within minutes of credit, minimal balance retention, and common device linkage. What is this and how do you respond?
entries.text: This is a **mule account network**. The red flags are clear. Small-value inward transfers from unrelated sources, rapid outward movement within minutes of credit, minimal balance retention, and common device or IP linkage across accounts. One account with this pattern is a case. Linked accounts with the same pattern are a network. I act fast. A **debit freeze** on the suspect accounts stops the

entries.title: Where does sanctions screening fit in the payment flow, and how do you design it so it does not slow down real time payments?
entries.text: Sanctions screening sits in the payment flow between validation and routing, and it must be fast enough not to break real time payments. The flow is: the channel sends the instruction to the hub, the hub extracts the **debtor name, creditor name, and any address fields**, and sends them to the screening engine. The engine compares them against sanctions lists and returns a result: clear,

entries.title: Transaction monitoring flags an account that receives several small transfers from unrelated people, then sends the full amount abroad within an hour. Explain the pattern, what it suggests, and what the bank does next.
entries.text: This is a classic **money mule** pattern. The account receives multiple small **inward transfers** from people who have no connection to the account holder, and then sends the money out almost immediately, usually to an account abroad. The small amounts are designed to stay below the **monitoring thresholds**, and the speed is designed to move the money before the bank can react. The pattern

entries.title: A sanctions list is updated at midday and a new name is added. Several payments are already in flight that involve that name. Explain what the bank must do with the payments that are already moving.
entries.text: When a **sanctions list** is updated, the new entry applies **immediately**. The bank must screen all payments against the updated list, including payments that are already in flight. The first step is to identify which payments are affected: the bank checks the **payment queue** for payments sent but not yet settled and payments received but not yet credited. Any payment that matches must be

entries.title: A customer calls in tears. They were tricked by a fraudster posing as their bank into sending 15,000 pounds to a criminal account. Explain how the bank handles the case, what the customer can expect, and what the bank does to try to recover the money.
entries.text: This is **authorised push payment fraud**, where the customer was tricked into authorising the payment themselves. The bank must act with **empathy** first: the customer is a victim, and the first thing they need is to be believed and to be told what will happen next. The bank must immediately contact the **receiving bank** and ask it to freeze the criminal account, because the fraudster moves

entries.title: A customer makes cash deposits of 9,500 pounds every few days, always just below the 10,000 pound reporting threshold. Explain what the bank suspects, how it investigates, and what happens if the suspicion is confirmed.
entries.text: The bank suspects **structuring**, which is the deliberate splitting of transactions to avoid a **reporting threshold**. The threshold exists so that large cash transactions are reported to the authorities, and a customer who consistently deposits just below it is likely trying to avoid that report. The pattern is suspicious because there is no normal business reason to deposit 9,500 pounds

entries.title: A payment is held because the beneficiary name fuzzy matches a sanctions list entry. The name is a common one, like Mohammed Khan, and the customer is angry about the delay. Explain fuzzy matching, why the payment was held, and how it gets released.
entries.text: **Fuzzy matching** is the technique sanctions screening systems use to catch names that are spelled differently, transliterated from another alphabet, or entered with a typo. The system does not look for an exact match. It looks for names that are **similar enough** to be the same person, and it scores the similarity. A common name like Mohammed Khan will match many entries on a sanctions list,

entries.title: A bank trade finance team notices that the invoice value for a shipment of electronics is three times the market price, and the goods are shipped through three countries for no clear reason. Explain trade based money laundering and how the bank responds.
entries.text: **Trade based money laundering** is the use of international trade to move criminal money across borders by disguising it as legitimate business. The techniques include **over invoicing**, where the invoice value is inflated so that extra money moves with the shipment, **under invoicing**, where the value is reduced, and **phantom shipments**, where the goods do not exist at all. In this case,

entries.title: A customer adds a new payee to their online banking, then immediately sends a large payment to that payee. The bank transaction monitoring flags it. Explain what the bank suspects and what controls should have stopped it.
entries.text: The bank suspects **account takeover**. A fraudster has gained access to the customer account, added a new payee, which is an account the fraudster controls, and then sent a large payment to it. The pattern is a red flag because genuine customers rarely add a payee and send a large payment in the same session. The controls that should have stopped it include **strong customer authentication**

entries.title: A customer wants to send a large payment to a cryptocurrency exchange. The bank compliance team is unsure whether to allow it. Explain the risks, what the bank should check, and how it makes the decision.
entries.text: A payment to a **cryptocurrency exchange** carries specific risks. Cryptocurrency can be used to move money quickly and anonymously, which makes it attractive for **money laundering**, **fraud**, and **sanctions evasion**. The bank must check several things before it allows the payment. First, is the exchange **regulated** and does it carry out **customer due diligence** on its own users. A

entries.title: Walk through a clean card payment, from the customer tapping the card to the merchant being settled. What happens at authorisation, clearing, and settlement?
entries.text: A card payment has three stages, authorisation, clearing, and settlement, and in a clean flow each one happens on time. The customer taps their card, and the merchant sends an **authorisation request** to the acquiring bank. The acquirer routes it through the card scheme to the issuing bank. The issuing bank checks the balance, the card status, and the fraud rules, then approves the transaction

entries.title: A customer taps their card at a cafe and the terminal declines it, even though they have plenty of money in the account. The customer is embarrassed and angry. How do you investigate the decline and what do you tell the customer?
entries.text: Start with the **authorisation response code**, because it tells you exactly why the issuer said no. A code like **05 do not honour** is a generic issuer decline, **51** means insufficient funds, **54** means an expired card, and **91** means the issuer is temporarily unavailable. Ask the merchant for the code from the terminal receipt or the acquirer log before you guess anything. Next, check

entries.title: A merchant receives a chargeback 60 days after a sale. The reason code says the cardholder did not authorise the transaction, but the merchant has signed delivery proof and a photo of the goods being handed over. How does the merchant fight the chargeback, and what are the chances?
entries.text: The merchant fights it through **representment**, which is the formal reply to a chargeback sent through the acquirer to the card scheme. The acquirer has a strict deadline, usually **30 to 45 days** from the chargeback date, and missing it means the money is lost automatically, so the first step is to confirm the deadline and start the clock. The merchant must submit **compelling evidence**: the

entries.title: A small retailer has not received card settlement for two days. Takings were normal, the terminal shows the sales went through, but no money has arrived in the bank account. Walk through how you find the problem.
entries.text: Start by checking whether the terminal **batched and closed** for those two days. Card payments are authorised in real time, but they are only sent for clearing when the terminal closes its **batch**, usually at end of day. If the batch was never closed, the money is sitting authorised but uncleared, and closing the batch releases it. Next, ask the acquirer to confirm it received the **clearing

entries.title: An online shopper starts a purchase, gets a 3-D Secure challenge on their phone, fails it twice, and abandons the checkout. The merchant loses the sale and blames the bank. Explain what happened and how the merchant reduces abandoned checkouts without increasing fraud.
entries.text: The shopper hit **3-D Secure**, the extra authentication step that asks the cardholder to confirm the payment, usually through their banking app or a one time passcode. Failing it twice means the issuer could not verify the shopper, so the payment was not authenticated and the merchant correctly did not proceed. Under **PSD2 strong customer authentication** rules, the issuer must challenge

entries.title: Your bank stores card numbers for one-click checkout. The team wants to move from stored PANs to network tokens. Explain what changes, what the risks are, and how you migrate without breaking existing customers.
entries.text: Moving to **network tokens** means replacing the stored **PAN**, the 16 digit card number, with a token issued by the card scheme, such as Visa or Mastercard. The token works like the card number for payments, but it is useless if stolen, because it only works with the merchant it was issued for and can be suspended without reissuing the card. The migration starts with the **token requestor**

entries.title: A customer taps their card several times during the day and suddenly the terminal asks for a PIN. They have never been asked for a PIN on contactless before. Explain why this happens and what the customer should do.
entries.text: This is the **contactless cumulative limit** doing its job. Under **strong customer authentication** rules, a card can only be used contactless for a certain total value, or a certain number of taps, before the terminal must ask for a **PIN** to prove the person holding the card is the real cardholder. In the UK the single tap limit is **100 pounds**, and the cumulative limit means that after

entries.title: A customer pays by card while on holiday abroad and later complains that the amount taken from their account is higher than the price on the receipt. The shop offered to charge them in their home currency. Explain what happened and what the customer should have done.
entries.text: The shop offered **dynamic currency conversion**, known as DCC, which means the card payment is converted into the customer home currency at the point of sale, using the exchange rate set by the merchant or their acquirer. That rate is almost always worse than the rate the card scheme, Visa or Mastercard, would apply, and it often includes an extra **markup** of 3 to 5 percent. The customer

entries.title: A card scheme raises its interchange rates. The acquirer passes the increase to merchants, and a large retailer threatens to leave. Explain what interchange is, why the merchant pays it, and how the acquirer handles the negotiation.
entries.text: **Interchange** is the fee the merchant bank, the acquirer, pays to the cardholder bank, the issuer, on every card transaction. It is the largest part of the **merchant service charge**, the total fee the merchant pays to accept cards, and it is set by the card scheme, not by the acquirer. The acquirer cannot remove it, it can only decide how much of its own margin to add on top. When the scheme

entries.title: An authorisation is approved at the till, the customer leaves with the goods, but the merchant settlement for that day is short by exactly that amount. The clearing file has no record of the transaction. What went wrong and how do you fix it?
entries.text: The authorisation and the clearing are two separate steps, and this case shows the second step failed. The card was authorised in real time, which is why the customer left with the goods, but the transaction was never **presented for clearing**. In a **dual message** system, the authorisation holds the funds and the clearing message, the presentment, actually moves the money. If the terminal

entries.title: A customer subscription payment fails the month after their card is reissued with a new expiry date. The customer did not update the card details with the merchant. Explain why the payment failed and how it should have worked.
entries.text: The payment failed because the merchant tried to charge the **old card details**. A reissued card has a new expiry date and sometimes a new card number, and the stored details the merchant holds are now out of date. The subscription should have kept working through the **account updater** service, run by Visa and Mastercard. When a card is reissued, the issuer sends the new details to the scheme,

entries.title: A merchant is charged more for card acceptance than expected. When you investigate, you find the merchant category code on the account is wrong. Explain what a merchant category code is, why it matters, and how you fix it.
entries.text: The **merchant category code**, or MCC, is a four digit code that describes what type of business the merchant is, such as a supermarket, a restaurant, or an airline. The code is set when the merchant account is opened, and it drives two things: the **interchange rate** the merchant pays, because different business types have different rates, and the **risk rules** applied to the account, because

entries.title: A fraudster uses a stolen card at a terminal. The chip fails to read, the terminal falls back to the magnetic stripe, and the transaction goes through. Who bears the loss, and what should the merchant and the acquirer have done?
entries.text: This is an **EMV fallback** transaction, where the chip could not be read and the terminal used the **magnetic stripe** instead. The magnetic stripe is easy to copy, which is why the industry moved to chip, and fallback transactions are a known fraud route. Under the **liability shift** rules, the party that has not adopted EMV bears the loss. If the merchant terminal is chip enabled but the card

entries.title: A customer returns goods to a shop and the refund is issued to a card that has since expired. The customer worries the money is lost. Explain where the refund goes and what the customer should expect.
entries.text: The money is not lost. When a refund is issued to an **expired card**, the issuer routes it using the card account behind the card number, not the plastic card itself. The card number stays linked to the same account even after the expiry date passes, so the refund lands in the account that the old card belonged to. If the customer has been issued a **replacement card**, the refund usually

entries.title: A new online merchant wants to start accepting card payments. The acquirer asks for business details, trading history, and a reserve. The merchant thinks this is unnecessary paperwork. Explain why the acquirer does this and what the merchant should expect.
entries.text: The acquirer is doing **merchant underwriting**, which is the risk check every acquirer must do before letting a business take card payments. Card payments carry a risk the acquirer takes on: if the merchant takes money and then fails to deliver the goods, or goes out of business, the acquirer must refund the cardholders through **chargebacks**. The acquirer therefore checks the business model,

entries.title: Explain the difference between single message and dual message card clearing, and why a merchant might be paid at a different time depending on which system their acquirer uses.
entries.text: In a **dual message** system, a card payment has two separate steps. The **authorisation** message checks the funds and holds the amount, and hours later a **clearing** message, the presentment, actually moves the money. Visa and Mastercard credit cards mostly work this way, and the merchant is paid after the clearing file is processed, usually the next working day. In a **single message**

entries.title: What is a payment exception queue?
entries.text: A payment exception queue is the worklist where payments that cannot be processed automatically are held for manual handling by operations staff. Payments land in the exception queue for many reasons: a sanctions screening alert, a failed validation such as an invalid account number, a missing beneficiary address, a limit breach, a liquidity shortfall, or a technical error such as a rejected

entries.title: What is a payment operations dashboard?
entries.text: A payment operations dashboard is a real-time view of payment processing health that lets operations teams see what is happening and act quickly when something goes wrong. It typically shows volumes by payment type, channel, and currency; the straight through processing rate; the size and ageing of exception queues; payments approaching cut-off times; settlement and nostro balances; and the

entries.title: What is a payment test case?
entries.text: A payment test case is a documented scenario that verifies a specific behavior of a payment system, with defined inputs, expected results, and pass or fail criteria. A good test case starts with a clear objective, for example verifying that a SEPA payment with an invalid IBAN is rejected with the correct error code. It specifies the preconditions, such as the test account setup and reference

entries.title: How does a large bank handle peak volumes on a salary day or month end?
entries.text: A large bank plans for peak days weeks in advance. The operations team looks at the calendar and knows which days will be heavy: month end, salary days, tax payment deadlines and the days before a public holiday. First, they check capacity. The payment hub, the core banking system and the clearing interfaces all have throughput limits, and the team confirms they can handle the expected volume.

entries.title: How are payments operations teams structured in a large bank?
entries.text: In a large bank like BNY Mellon or Goldman Sachs, payments operations is split into teams by function, not by product. The intake team receives payment files and instructions from channels and checks they are complete. The processing team monitors the payment hub and makes sure payments flow through without getting stuck. The exceptions team investigates payments that fail validation, get

entries.title: What happens when a payment is stuck in a queue at a large bank?
entries.text: A payment gets stuck in a queue when it cannot move to the next step. The most common reasons are a missing field, a failed validation, a sanctions hold or a system that is down. The payment hub holds the payment in a queue and flags it for the operations team. The operations team looks at the queue regularly during the day. They open the payment, read the error or the hold reason and decide what

entries.title: How does a large bank test a payment change before it goes live?
entries.text: Testing a payment change in a large bank has several layers because a defect can stop real money. First, the engineers run unit tests on the code they wrote. Second, the QA team runs system integration tests in a test environment that mirrors production, checking that the payment hub talks correctly to the core banking system, the sanctions screening and the clearing interfaces. Third, the BA

entries.title: What is the role of a payments operations manager during a system outage?
entries.text: When a payment system goes down, the operations manager becomes the incident owner. The first job is to assess the impact: which payments are affected, how many, and whether customers are impacted. The manager opens an incident, calls the engineering team and the duty manager, and starts a bridge call. Second, the manager decides whether to stop taking new payments or to queue them. Stopping

entries.title: How does a bank handle a failed file from a corporate client?
entries.text: A corporate client sends a payment file, usually a bulk file with hundreds or thousands of payments. The bank's file gateway receives the file and checks it. First, it checks the file format: is it a valid file, does it have the right structure, are the headers correct. If the format is wrong, the whole file is rejected and the client is told to fix it and resend. Second, it checks each payment

entries.title: How does a large bank measure payment performance and what are the key metrics?
entries.text: A large bank tracks payment performance with a small set of metrics that everyone watches. The first is the straight-through processing rate: the percentage of payments that go through without manual intervention. A high STP rate means the system is working well. The second is the average processing time: how long from instruction to settlement. For instant payments this is measured in seconds,

entries.title: A corporate customer submits a payment one minute after the cut-off. The channel accepts it, but the clearing system rejects it because the settlement window has closed. The customer expects same-day value. What do you do?
entries.text: A cut-off is a contract between the bank, the clearing system, and every downstream batch. When a payment misses it, the channel and the clearing system disagree, and the customer is caught in between. I first check the **pacs.002** status to confirm the rejection and the reason. If the payment was rejected pre-settlement, no funds have moved, so I can repair and resubmit for the next value date.

entries.title: Customers report duplicate debits, but no alerts fired. The root cause is a messaging failure, the broker acknowledged a message before replication finished, then died, and the retry charged again. How do you debug this?
entries.text: The failure is in the interaction between systems, not in any single component, which is why no alert fired. Each part behaved as designed. The producer used **acks equals 1**, so only the leader broker acknowledged the message. The broker died before replication finished, so the message was lost. But the payment had already been charged, and the system believed it had failed, so the retry

entries.title: A payment timeout keeps recurring but the network is healthy and the servers look fine. Where do you look for the root cause?
entries.text: The timeout is the symptom, not the cause. I stop fixating on where the error surfaced and start from where the message was created. I trace the **full end-to-end lifecycle** hop by hop, with timestamps and message copies at every step. In this kind of case the real culprit is often a small deviation from **message standards** upstream, not an infrastructure problem. A field that is slightly out

entries.title: A release passes QA, staging, and a small rollout. Hours after full release, volumes spike and failures spike with them. What went wrong?
entries.text: Testing never hit the fringe edge case. The root cause was one parameter that everyone assumed was always populated, but in a small number of real cases it came back empty. QA, staging, and a small rollout all passed because the edge case only appeared at full volume. The cascade was fast. **Partner API calls failed**, reconciliation mismatched, and war rooms opened with stakeholders. Recovery

entries.title: Payments fail intermittently, but only during peak hours. The system is fine at all other times. How do you find the root cause?
entries.text: I run the **5-Why chain** from the symptom down. The payments time out, so why. Processing is slow, so why. Database queries are lagging, so why. Server load is high, so why. The servers are not sized for peak traffic. That chain points at capacity, not code. **Peak-only failures mean capacity**. All-day failures mean code or data. I fix the root, not the symptom. I add **database indexing** on

entries.title: A payment left the channel but never arrived at the clearing house. The customer is asking where their money is. How do you trace it and what do you tell them?
entries.text: Start by checking the **pacs.002** status reports. If the clearing house sent an ACSC, the payment settled and the problem is in the feedback loop. If there is no pacs.002, the payment never reached the clearing house. Next, check the **payment hub logs** for that UETR. The hub records every hop: received from channel, validated, sent to clearing. Find the last hop that succeeded. Then check the

entries.title: A corporate customer sends a bulk file with 5,000 salary payments. Walk through how the file is processed without errors, from receipt to settlement.
entries.text: A clean bulk file starts before the file even arrives. The corporate customer prepares a **pain.001** file with hundreds or thousands of payments, and the bank publishes a clear file specification so the customer knows the exact format. When the file arrives, the hub validates the file structure first, checking the header, the record count, and the control totals. Then it validates each payment

entries.title: A customer submits a payment at 3 PM and the cut-off is 4 PM. Walk through how the payment meets the cut-off and settles on the same value date.
entries.text: Meeting the cut-off works because the whole chain is aligned to the same clock. The customer submits the payment before the published **cut-off time**, and the channel accepts it. The payment hub validates it immediately and sends the **pacs.008** to the clearing system before the clearing cut-off. The clearing system processes it in the current settlement cycle, and the beneficiary bank credits

entries.title: A corporate customer sends a payment file that passes validation on the first attempt. What does the bank do to make first-time-right files the norm?
entries.text: A file that passes validation the first time is a sign that the customer onboarding and the file specification both work. The corporate customer prepares the file using the bank's **published specification**, which defines the exact format, the mandatory fields, and the validation rules. Before sending the file, the customer runs it through the bank's **pre-validation tool**, which checks the

entries.title: Walk through a clean bulk salary run. How does an employer pay 5,000 employees on payday with every payment landing on time?
entries.text: A clean salary run works because the file, the funding, and the timing are all agreed in advance. The employer sends a **pain.001** file with every employee payment, the account numbers, the amounts, and the value date, which is payday. The bank validates the file, checking each payment against the account details and the sanctions lists. The bank checks that the employer account has **enough

entries.title: A production incident hits during a release. What is your role?
entries.text: My role in a production incident is to own the business impact and the communication, while engineering owns the technical fix. First, I find out what is affected: which payments, how many customers, whether money is stuck or just delayed. I write this down clearly so everyone is working from the same facts. Second, I join the incident bridge and stay on it, translating between engineering and

entries.title: How do you prioritise when five payment issues land at once?
entries.text: I triage by impact first, then by urgency. I look at all five issues and ask three questions about each one: how many customers are affected, is money stuck or at risk, and is there a deadline like a cut off or a regulatory report. The issue that affects the most customers and has money at risk comes first. I am explicit about the order and I tell the stakeholders what I am working on and what is

entries.title: A payment is failing in production and nobody knows why. Walk me through your investigation.
entries.text: I start with the facts, not guesses. First, I find a failing payment and get its reference number and UETR. I check the payment hub to see where it stopped and what error was recorded. I look at the message that was sent and the response that came back. If the response is a pacs.002 rejection, I read the reason code: it tells me exactly what failed. Second, I check whether the failure is isolated

entries.title: A user acceptance test fails on the last day before go-live. What do you do?
entries.text: I would not sign off a go live with a failing test on the last day. First, I find out what failed and how serious it is. Is it a defect that stops payments, or a minor display issue. If it stops payments or risks wrong payments, the go live must be delayed or the scope reduced. entries.title: A test environment does not match production. How do you handle it?
entries.text: A test environment that does not match production is a common and dangerous problem, because a test can pass and the change can still fail in production. First, I identify the differences: is the data different, is the configuration different, is a system missing or a different version. entries.title: How do you prepare for a payment system cutover weekend?
entries.text: A cutover weekend is planned in detail because the bank cannot afford to get it wrong. The preparation starts weeks before. I write the cutover plan with every step, who does it, how long it takes and what the rollback is. I run a dress rehearsal in a test environment following the exact steps, and I time each step to confirm the plan fits in the window. I prepare the test scenarios for the go

entries.title: What controls does a large bank put around payments to manage risk?
entries.text: A large bank layers controls around payments because the risk is real money leaving the bank. The first control is authentication: the person giving the instruction must prove who they are, through a password, a token or a biometric. The second is authorisation: the payment must be approved by someone with the right limit, and large payments need two approvers. The third is sanctions screening:

entries.title: A stakeholder wants a change that breaks a regulatory rule. What do you do?
entries.text: I would not agree to it, but I would not just say no either. First I would understand what the stakeholder actually needs. Often the request that breaks a rule is a shortcut to a genuine business need, and there is a compliant way to meet that need. I would explain the rule in plain language: what the regulation says, why it exists and what happens if the bank breaks it, including fines and

entries.title: A regulatory change lands with a tight deadline. How do you respond?
entries.text: A regulatory change with a tight deadline is a common situation in payments. First, I read the regulation and the regulator's guidance to understand exactly what must change and by when. I do not rely on a summary from someone else. Second, I assess the impact: which payment types are affected, which systems, which customer journeys and which reports. I map the change to the current process and

entries.title: How do you handle a situation where the business and compliance disagree?
entries.text: When the business and compliance disagree, the BA is in the middle and has to help both sides reach a decision that is compliant and workable. First, I make sure I understand both positions precisely. The business usually wants speed or simplicity for the customer. Compliance wants the control that protects the bank and meets the regulation. I write down both positions and the underlying reason

entries.title: A customer tries to pay online and the bank asks them to approve the payment in their banking app. The customer complains that this is an extra step and asks why it is needed. Explain strong customer authentication under PSD2 and when the bank can skip it.
entries.text: **Strong customer authentication**, or SCA, is a requirement under **PSD2**, the European payment services law. It means the customer must prove their identity using at least two of three factors: something they know, such as a password, something they have, such as their phone, and something they are, such as a fingerprint. entries.title: Your bank operates in the euro area. The Instant Payments Regulation now requires you to offer SEPA Instant payments and to check the payee name before sending. Explain what the regulation requires and what your bank must build to comply.
entries.text: The **Instant Payments Regulation** requires banks in the euro area to offer **SEPA Instant Credit Transfer**, or SCT Inst, so that customers can send and receive euro payments within **10 seconds**, 24 hours a day, every day of the year. The bank must also offer instant payments at a price no higher than a standard credit transfer, which means it cannot charge a premium for speed. The second

entries.title: Your bank payment platform goes down for four hours during a busy morning. The regulator asks for a report under the operational resilience rules. Explain what DORA requires, what the bank must show, and how the operations team prepares for this.
entries.text: **DORA**, the Digital Operational Resilience Act, requires financial firms in the EU to be able to withstand, respond to, and recover from technology disruptions. A four hour payment outage is exactly the kind of incident DORA covers. The bank must report the incident to the regulator within a strict timeline, usually an **initial notification within 4 hours** and a fuller report within 72 hours,

entries.title: A customer is tricked by a fraudster into sending 20,000 pounds to a criminal account. The customer reports it to the bank the same day. Under the UK PSR rules on authorised push payment fraud, who pays, and what does the bank have to do?
entries.text: Under the **PSR reimbursement rules**, the sending bank must reimburse the customer for **authorised push payment fraud**, where the customer was tricked into authorising the payment. The cost is split **50/50** between the sending bank and the receiving bank, unless the receiving bank can show it did not meet its obligations. entries.title: The SWIFT CBPR+ migration deadline has passed and MT messages are no longer accepted for cross border payments. A small bank in your network is still sending MT103 messages. What happens to those messages and what must the bank do?
entries.text: When the **CBPR+ migration** deadline passes, the SWIFT network stops accepting **MT103** messages for cross border payments and requires **ISO 20022** messages, such as the **pacs.008**. An MT103 sent after the deadline is **rejected** by the network, and the sending bank receives a rejection notice. entries.title: A payment is blocked because the beneficiary name matches a name on the OFAC sanctions list. The customer says it is a different person with the same name. Explain what happens next and why the bank cannot simply release the payment.
entries.text: **OFAC**, the US Office of Foreign Assets Control, maintains the **SDN list**, a list of people and entities that US persons and banks must not deal with. When a payment matches a name on the list, the bank must **block** it, which means holding the funds and not releasing them, while it investigates. entries.title: A customer asks why the bank needs their full address for a cross border payment, and whether the bank is sharing their personal data. Explain the GDPR position and what the bank must do with payment data.
entries.text: Under **GDPR**, the bank can only collect and use personal data when it has a **lawful basis**. For a cross border payment, the lawful basis is that the data is necessary to perform the contract, the payment instruction, and to comply with a **legal obligation**, because payment regulations require the bank to include the payer name, account, and address in the payment message. entries.title: Transaction monitoring flags a customer who has received several cash deposits just below the reporting threshold, then sent the money abroad. Explain what the bank suspects, what it must do, and what it must never tell the customer.
entries.text: The bank suspects **structuring**, which is the deliberate splitting of transactions into smaller amounts to avoid a reporting threshold. It is a classic **money laundering** technique: the criminal breaks a large sum into deposits just below the threshold, so no single transaction triggers a report, then moves the money abroad where it is harder to trace. entries.title: The Bank of England migrates CHAPS to ISO 20022. A corporate customer asks what changes for them. Explain the migration, what the customer must do, and what improves once it is live.
entries.text: The **Bank of England** migrated **CHAPS**, the UK high value payment system, to **ISO 20022** message formats. The change means CHAPS payments now use the same structured data standard as the rest of the world, instead of the older MT format. entries.title: An Indian company wants to pay a supplier in Germany. The payment is delayed because the bank asks for FEMA documentation. Explain what FEMA is, why the bank asks, and what the company should prepare.
entries.text: **FEMA**, the Foreign Exchange Management Act, is the Indian law that governs how money moves in and out of India. It requires that cross border payments are made for a **permitted purpose**, that the amount is genuine, and that the transaction is reported to the **Reserve Bank of India** through the bank. entries.title: A bank receives a payment instruction where the beneficiary information is missing. The payment cannot be processed. Explain the travel rule and what the bank must do.
entries.text: The **travel rule** requires that certain information about the payer and the payee **travels with** the payment, from the sending bank all the way to the beneficiary bank. Under the EU **Funds Transfer Regulation**, the payer information must include the name, the account number, and the address, and the payee information must include the name and the account number. entries.title: Your bank has identified its payment platform as a critical business service under the operational resilience rules. The board asks what impact tolerance means and what happens if it is breached. Explain it in plain language.
entries.text: **Impact tolerance** is the maximum disruption the bank is willing to accept for a **critical business service** before the harm to customers, to the market, or to the bank itself becomes unacceptable. entries.title: What is a payment workshop and what questions do you ask?
entries.text: A payment workshop is a facilitated session where a BA brings business stakeholders, operations staff, and technical teams together to define requirements for a payment change. It is more effective than one-to-one interviews for payments because a payment flow crosses many teams, and a workshop surfaces disagreements early. entries.title: How does a BA work with engineering and operations in a large bank?
entries.text: A BA in a large bank is the bridge between the business and the engineers. The work starts with operations. The BA sits with the operations team and watches how they process payments today, where they struggle and what they need. entries.title: How is a change delivered in a large bank: release, testing and cutover?
entries.text: Change in a large bank follows a strict path because a mistake can stop payments for thousands of customers. First, the change is designed and the requirements are written and signed off by the business, operations and risk. Second, the engineers build it in a development environment. entries.title: How does a large bank onboard a new corporate client onto its payment platform?
entries.text: Onboarding a corporate client onto a payment platform is a project that takes weeks, not days. First, the bank does due diligence: it checks the client's identity, its business, its owners and its risk profile. entries.title: What is the role of a business analyst in a payments transformation programme?
entries.text: A payments transformation programme in a large bank replaces old systems with new ones, often moving from legacy mainframe payment engines to a modern payment hub. The BA is central to this work. First, the BA documents the current state: how payments work today, which systems are involved, where the manual workarounds are and what breaks. entries.title: You have two conflicting requirements from operations and engineering. How do you resolve it?
entries.text: I would start by bringing both sides into the same room with the facts in front of them. Operations wants the payment to be processed a certain way because that is how their team works today. entries.title: How do you gather requirements for a new payment product?
entries.text: I start by understanding the problem the product is solving, not the solution someone has already imagined. I talk to the business sponsor and ask: who is the customer, what payment are they making, what goes wrong today, what does good look like. entries.title: How do you explain a complex payment failure to a non-technical stakeholder?
entries.text: I start with the outcome, not the technical detail. I would say: the payment did not reach the beneficiary on time, and here is what that means for the customer. Then I explain the cause in plain terms, using an analogy if it helps. For example, I might say: think of the payment like a letter. entries.title: How do you handle a requirement that keeps changing?
entries.text: Changing requirements are normal in payments because the business learns as the build progresses. I handle it by making the change process visible and controlled. First, I understand the change: what is different, why is it needed, and what is the impact on what is already built. entries.title: A vendor delivers a payment component late. What do you do?
entries.text: First, I assess the impact: what is delayed, who is affected and whether there is a workaround. I tell the stakeholders immediately so they hear it from me, not from a missed deadline. Second, I understand the reason for the delay from the vendor: is it a resource problem, a technical blocker or a scope misunderstanding. I ask for specifics, not a vague new date. entries.title: How do you validate that a payment requirement is complete?
entries.text: I validate a requirement by testing it against real examples. First, I take a real payment and walk it through the requirement end to end: does the requirement cover every step, every field, every decision point and every error. entries.title: How do you work with a difficult stakeholder?
entries.text: I start by understanding what the stakeholder actually cares about, not what they are demanding. A difficult stakeholder is often someone under pressure from their own manager or client, and the demand is a symptom of that pressure. entries.title: How do you document a payment flow for both business and technical readers?
entries.text: I write two versions of the same flow, because business and technical readers need different things. For the business reader, I write a simple step by step flow in plain language: the customer gives the instruction, the bank checks it, the bank sends it, the beneficiary receives it. entries.text: I found it during user acceptance testing, before go live, which is exactly when you want to find it. We were testing a new payment type and the test scenario was a payment with a special character in the beneficiary name. entries.text: I had a stakeholder who wanted a new payment feature built in two weeks, but the design needed six weeks because it touched the sanctions screening and the reconciliation. entries.text: I noticed that the exceptions team was spending a large part of their day manually correcting payments that failed because the beneficiary account number had a space or a dash in it. entries.title: Tell me about a time you had to learn a new payment system quickly.
entries.text: I was asked to work on a new instant payments system that I had never used before. I started by reading the scheme rules and the message specifications so I understood the standard. entries.title: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager about a payment design.
entries.text: My manager wanted to build a new payment feature as a custom addition to the existing system. I thought that was the wrong approach because the existing system was already hard to maintain, and adding a custom feature would make it worse. I did not just disagree in a meeting. entries.text: During a testing cycle, I noticed that the test scenarios only covered payments where the beneficiary bank was in the same country. entries.title: In a job interview for a payments business analyst role, the interviewer says: tell me about yourself. How do you structure a strong answer that is not just a list of your jobs?
entries.text: Use a simple three part structure: **present, past, future**. Start with the present: what you do now, in one sentence, such as I am a senior business analyst working on payments transformation at a large bank. entries.title: The interviewer asks: tell me about the biggest payments failure you have handled. How do you answer honestly without making yourself look bad?
entries.text: Use the **STAR** structure: situation, task, action, result. Describe the situation briefly, such as a cross border payment of 125,000 pounds that vanished between banks and the customer was waiting. Explain your task: to find the payment, keep the customer informed, and prevent a repeat. entries.title: The interviewer asks why you are leaving your current bank. You are unhappy there, but you know you should not criticise your employer. How do you answer?
entries.text: Keep the answer **forward looking**, not backward looking. Talk about what you want to move towards, not what you want to escape from. A good answer is: I have learned a great deal in my current role, I have built deep experience in payments operations and ISO 20022, and now I want to apply that experience to a larger transformation programme, which is what this role offers. entries.title: The hiring manager is not technical. They ask you to explain ISO 20022 migration in plain language. How do you explain it without jargon?
entries.text: Start with an analogy the manager already understands. Say: imagine every bank in the world writes payment instructions in a different language, and ISO 20022 is the agreement to use one common language. entries.title: The interviewer asks about your salary expectations. You do not want to price yourself out, but you also do not want to accept less than you are worth. How do you handle the question?
entries.text: Do your **research** before the interview. Find out the market rate for the role, the location, and your experience level, using salary surveys, job adverts, and conversations with recruiters. When the question comes, give a **range**, not a single number, and anchor the range to the market and to your experience. A good answer is: based on the market for this role and my experience in payments

entries.text: Pick a real example where a stakeholder disagreed with you and you resolved it professionally. Use the **STAR** structure. entries.text: Give a **specific** answer, not a vague one. Name the sources you actually use: the **SWIFT** standards releases and the CBPR+ usage guidelines, the **Bank of England** and **European Payments Council** publications, the **PSR** and **FCA** updates, and the industry newsletters you read regularly. entries.text: Start by stating your **framework**, then apply it. A good framework is: regulatory deadlines first, because missing them means fines and the risk of losing the ability to operate; revenue second, because it funds the business; and operational fixes third, unless the operations problem is causing customer harm or financial loss. entries.title: The interviewer asks how you would handle a production incident where payments are failing and nobody knows why. Walk through your answer.
entries.text: Show a calm, structured approach. First, **assess the impact**: how many payments are failing, which customers are affected, and whether money is at risk. Second, **communicate**: tell the operations manager, the incident team, and the customer service team what is happening, so nobody is guessing. entries.title: At the end of the interview, the interviewer asks if you have any questions. What should you ask, and what should you avoid asking?
entries.text: Ask questions that show you are **genuinely interested** in the role and that you have done your **research**. Good questions are: what does success look like in this role in the first six months; what is the biggest challenge facing the payments programme right now; how does the team work with operations and engineering; and what is the plan for the ISO 20022 migration or the next major change.
